title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
hook: a spear, and the eyewitness insists: he saw it

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Greek word from the cross, tetelestai. Your line: a debt paid, a victory won.

John usually tells his story in a calm, steady voice. Then, right after the death of Jesus, the narrator does something unusual. He steps almost into the frame and speaks straight to you. I'm not making this up, he says, in effect. Someone saw it. And he's telling you so that you will believe. It's like a documentary where the person holding the camera turns it around for a moment.

It's the day of preparation, and the next day is a Sabbath, a high day. The bodies can't be left on the crosses into it. So the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies taken down. Soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. Then they come to him. In the King James Bible: "But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs: But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water." Then the unusual line: "And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe." Bare record means testified. The Greek verb is martyreo, to bear witness. It's where our word martyr comes from: a martyr was first of all a witness. Why does John stress this so hard? Some early Christians taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body, and only seemed to die. Some scholars think John is answering that: real spear, real wound, real death, and someone standing there. John also hears two scriptures. A bone of him shall not be broken: the rule for the Passover lamb. And from the prophet Zechariah: they shall look on him whom they pierced. Then there's the blood and the water itself. John doesn't explain it. Early church writers like Augustine and John Chrysostom saw in it the two great signs of the church: the water of baptism and the blood of Communion. Others read it as simple evidence of death. The text leaves it there, with a witness.
screen: `A HIGH DAY: LEGS BROKEN, BUT NOT HIS.`
`REAL BODY, REAL DEATH, A REAL WITNESS.`
then, large: `HE THAT SAW IT BARE RECORD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who told you about something they saw or lived through, a grandparent's war story, a friend's account of how they were treated, a coworker who said something was wrong, and you didn't quite take it in. Bring their face to mind and hear their words again, slowly, as if they were telling the truth, because they may have been. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, simply honor them in your mind.
Martyreo. The Greek verb meaning to bear witness, the root of our word martyr: what the eyewitness did at the cross.
Your line: he who saw it. Someone was standing there, and said so. That's today's walk.

original.note: Greek: he has borne witness. from martyreo; the root of the word martyr.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome detail.
what it means: the narrator steps forward and insists: someone saw this, a real death, so that you might believe.
what a scholar hears: martyreo, and two scriptures: the Passover lamb's unbroken bones (Exodus 12:46) and Zechariah 12:10, 'they shall look on him whom they pierced'.

chat.says: Why does John stop the story to say someone saw the spear and the blood?
options: He insists on a real witness to a real wound and death, so ye might believe.
He wanted to prove the soldiers broke Jesus's legs like the other two.
He's saying the witness was Pilate, who wrote it all down for Rome.
chat.meaning: John 19:35: he that saw it bare record, and his record is true, that ye might believe. Real body, real death, a real witness.

martyreo.meaning: Greek: to bear witness; the root of martyr

Zechariah.meaning: a prophet: they shall look on him whom they pierced

Augustine.meaning: an early church writer who saw baptism and Communion here

John Chrysostom.meaning: an early church writer who also saw two signs of the church here

notes: 'The authorities ask Pilate' paraphrases 'the Jews therefore... besought Pilate' (19:31); chosen to avoid collective framing. Confirm.
Docetism as background to John's emphasis: a common scholarly suggestion, stated as 'many scholars think'. Confirm.
'A bone of him shall not be broken' (19:36): usually traced to Exodus 12:46 / Numbers 9:12, also Psalm 34:20. Confirm.
Augustine (Tractate 120 on John) and Chrysostom (Baptismal Instruction 3.17–19): blood and water as Eucharist and baptism. Confirm references.
howItsDone: Sacred Heart and Divine Mercy image (rays of red and pale light) draw on John 19:34. Confirm.
